theme: Saul’s death; David made king; the ark journey
readingInstruction: Read 1 Chronicles 10:1-13:14. Chronicles passes over Saul’s life and tells only his death, then moves quickly to David’s anointing as king over all Israel. Read for what the Chronicler chooses to emphasize.
settingTheScene: The Chronicler’s story begins with the death of Saul, which he gives a theological explanation: Saul died for his unfaithfulness. Then, in a single move, “all Israel” gathers at Hebron to make David king. The Chronicler skips David’s years as a fugitive and his seven-year reign over Judah. He wants to show a unified nation under God’s chosen king, with David’s first act being to capture Jerusalem and bring the ark there.
observation: “So Saul died for his breach of faith. He broke faith with the LORD in that he did not keep the command of the LORD” (10:13).
“And he did not seek guidance from the LORD. Therefore the LORD put him to death” (10:14).
“Then all Israel gathered to David at Hebron and said, Behold, we are your bone and flesh” (11:1).
“And the LORD your God said to you, You shall be shepherd of my people Israel” (11:2).
“And David became greater and greater, for the LORD of hosts was with him” (11:9).
“These were the chiefs of David’s mighty men, who gave him strong support in his kingdom” (11:10).
“And David said to all the assembly of Israel, If it seems good to you, and from the LORD our God… let us bring again the ark of our God to us” (13:2-3).
“And Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark… and God struck him down because he put out his hand to the ark” (13:9-10).
interpretation:
The Chronicler’s judgment on Saul is one sentence: he broke faith and he did not seek the LORD. That is the key. The central question of Chronicles is whether the kings “sought the LORD.” This phrase recurs throughout the books and is the test of every reign. Saul did not. David did.

The story shifts to David at Hebron, where all the tribes come together. Notice the key phrase: the LORD said, “You shall be shepherd of my people.” David’s reign is a gift from God. Jerusalem is taken, and the Chronicler stresses that David’s power grew because “the LORD of hosts was with him.” The list of mighty men follows, each of whom contributed to the kingdom. Chapter 12 describes the soldiers who came from all the tribes: “all of one mind to make David king.” Unity around God’s king is a major theme.

Then David consults with the leaders about the ark, which had been neglected since the days of Eli. “Let us bring again the ark of our God to us, for we did not seek it in the days of Saul.” The ark was the symbol of God’s presence, and bringing it to Jerusalem would make the city the spiritual center.

But the first attempt fails. They put the ark on a new cart, as the Philistines had done, rather than carry it on the shoulders of Levites as the law prescribed. When the oxen stumble, Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark and dies on the spot. It is a shocking moment. David is angry and afraid. The lesson is that good intentions are not enough. God’s presence is holy, and it must be approached on his terms. The ark is left at the house of Obed-edom for three months, and that house is blessed.
connection: Hebrews 12:28-29 says our God is a consuming fire, and we should offer acceptable worship with reverence and awe. John 4:24 says true worshipers worship in spirit and truth. Matthew 2:6 quotes Micah on the shepherd of Israel, and John 10:11 says Jesus is the good shepherd. Ephesians 4:3-6 urges unity of the Spirit. Leviticus 10:1-3 and Numbers 4:15 show the holiness of sacred things. 1 Samuel 13:13-14 records Saul’s disobedience.
application:
Ask yourself how you seek the LORD in your decisions, not after the fact but before.

Think about approaching God with reverence. Is there any casualness in your worship that needs correcting?

Pray for unity among believers around Christ.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to make you one who seeks him, as David did.
Confess where you have gone your own way.
